blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for the FY 2020/21 has been prepared in line with Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit to Parliament quarterly budget implementation reports for the national and county governments every four months.

During the reporting period, receipts into the consolidated fund amounted to Kshs.2.82 trillion, representing 95.6 per cent of the revised annual target of Kshs.2.95 trillion, a growth of 9 per cent compared to the Kshs.2.58 trillion received in the FY 2019/20. Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) has attributed the increase in revenue to sustained compliance efforts, revenue enhancement initiatives and improved voluntary compliance by taxpayers.

Total exchequer issues to the MDAs, Consolidated Fund Service (CFS) and County Governments amounted to Kshs.2.80 trillion representing 94.9 per cent of the revised net estimates, a growth compared to 92.5 per cent recorded in the FY 2019/20. The exchequer issues comprised of Kshs.372.49 billion for development expenditure, Kshs.2.04 trillion for recurrent expenditure and Kshs.379.51 billion to the County Governments representing 91.1 per cent, 94.8 per cent and 99.2 per cent of the revised net estimates. However, exchequer issues to county governments included Kshs.29.72 billion as equitable share arrears from FY 2019/20.

The total expenditure by the national government amounted to Kshs.2.59 trillion; representing 85.4 per cent of the revised gross estimates, a slight decline compared to 86.6 per cent recorded in the FY 2019/20. This comprised of development expenditure at Kshs.561.49 billion (absorption rate of 79.5 per cent), recurrent expenditure at Kshs.1.15 trillion (absorption rate of 91.5 per cent) and CFS expenditure at Kshs.878.78 billion (absorption rate of 82.1 per cent). Expenditure was supported through funding by the government and Ministerial Appropriation-in-Aid. (A-I-A)

Analysis of the development expenditure shows that Capital Transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) category recorded the highest expenditure at Kshs.323.81 billion representing 57.7 per cent of the gross expenditure. Transfers by the MDAs to SAGAs are meant to complement activities and mandates executed on behalf of parent ministries.

Review of the recurrent expenditure shows that a total of Kshs.498.07 billion was spent on compensation to employees representing 42.4 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs. This excludes personnel emoluments for Military payments and the National Intelligence Service. The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) recorded the highest expenditure on compensation to employees at Kshs.273.41 billion, translating to 55.9 per cent of total expenditure on compensation to employees by the national government. Further, some budget items recorded low levels of expenditure, which was attributed to the impact of the Corona Virus Disease (COVID -19) mitigation measures adopted by government to curb spread of the disease, namely Travelling, Training and Hospitality activities which are some of the major spending budget items by many MDAs.

The Office of the Controller of Budget identified several challenges that hindered effective budget implementation in the FY 2020/21. These included delays in submission of financial and non-financial reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget by some MDAs, non-adherence to end of year timelines, pending bills and high levels of public debt.

The report contains recommendations aimed at addressing the identified challenges. They include; submission of MDAs financial and non-financial performance reports to the OCOB within fifteen days following the end of each quarter; National Treasury to liaise with MDAs before effecting budget revisions; National Treasury to prepare the Supplementary Budget in good time and Parliament to consider and approve budget revisions in good time to allow for timely implementation of planned activities.

To check on the burden of public debt and other related fiscal strains, the government should enhance collection of domestic taxes to expand fiscal space and ensure borrowings are used only for financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure and at the minimum cost to reduce the high

cost associated with debt repayment. Further, the Controller of Budget recommends that the government takes stock of all ongoing and stalled projects, provide funds to finish them, and defers any new projects to curb the accumulation of pending bills. In addition, the government should oversee coordination of all joint projects between the two levels of government to avoid duplication of projects aimed at accomplishing similar objectives.

blocks.text: 1  INTRODUCTION

The OCoB is established under Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya and mandated to oversee the implementation of the budgets of the National and County Governments by authorizing withdrawals from public funds under Articles 204, 206 and 207 of the Constitution, and reporting on the implementation of the budgets to each House of Parliament every four months. This report fulfils the requirements of Article 228(6), of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016 by presenting progress on the budget implementation by the national government in the FY 2020/21.

The budget for the FY 2020/21, was prepared against a backdrop of limited fiscal space occasioned by revenue shortfalls and rising expenditure pressures. The Government focused on the need for fiscal consolidation to provide and maintain the necessary balance between revenues and expenditures while reducing the pace of the growth of public debt. Budget allocations in the 2020 Budget Policy Statement were realigned to the 'Big Four' Agenda as prioritized in the Medium-Term Plan Three (MTP III). Budgets of all MDAs curtailed spending on non-productive areas to ensure that public expenditures went to the most impactful programmes with the highest welfare benefits to Kenyans.

In implementing the FY 2020/21 budget activities, the National Treasury prepared two Supplementary budgets which were necessitated by the national government's need to match revenues to expenditures and to settle pending bills accrued by both the National and County governments. To unbundle the budget implementation and performance for the FY 2020/21 through this report, it is presented in eight chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter two presents the resource basket which was available to finance the budget and comprises revenue receipts into the Consolidated Fund and withdrawals approved by the COB. Chapter three presents the overall budget performance which includes a breakdown of budget spending identifying core spending areas, Consolidated Fund Services and Pending bills for the national government as of 30th June 2021.

Chapter four presents the financial performance by the sixty-eight MDAs which are grouped under the ten Sector working groups. The chapter presents a detailed analysis of sector performances showing allocations to specific MDAs as aligned to their key functions, exchequer issues to net estimates and actual expenditure to gross estimates presented as a percentage of the estimates. The net estimates do not include Appropriationsin- Aid (A-I-A) and present the budget to be funded by the government through the exchequer while the gross estimates include A-I-A. MDAs are classified into ten (10) Sectors according to the Classification of the Functions of the Government. The sectors are (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EI & ICT), (iv) Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR), (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA), (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO), (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR), (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR), sector.

Chapter five presents the budget performance by programmes giving the key drivers of the budget objectives, which encompass programmes and sub-programme performance by MDAs. Chapter six identifies key issues that the COB identified to be hampering effective budget implementation in the financial year. The chapter also makes recommendations aimed at addressing the issues identified as hampering efficient budget implementation. Chapter seven presents emerging issues that the COB has come across that need to be addressed to arrest future impropriety in relation to principles of public finance. Chapter eight provides the conclusion to the report.
The chapters are supported by annexes. A PDF version of the report is available on the COB website, https:// cob.go.ke.

2.2 Analysis of Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2 Analysis of Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: This section summarises the revenue estimates and receipts into the Consolidated Fund in the FY 2020/21. The Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and is the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes money that is reasonably excluded from the Fund by an Act of Parliament and payable into another public fund established for a specific purpose or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. The section also provides the trend of receipts into the Consolidated Fund over similar periods in the last five financial years.

blocks.text: 2.2.1  FY 2020/21 Revenue Estimates

The revised revenue estimates for the FY 2020/21 amounted to Kshs.2.94 trillion, an increase compared to Kshs.2.65 trillion budgeted in the FY 2019/20. To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, budgeted to raise revenue from various sources, which included: Tax revenue (Kshs.1.45 trillion), Non-tax revenue (Kshs.109.32 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.875.09 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.422.41 billion) and other Domestic financing at Kshs.22.81 billion.
2.2.2 Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

The receipts comprised of the opening balances from the previous financial year (FY 2019/20), Tax and non-tax revenues, Domestic borrowing, External Loans and Grants and other Domestic financing. 2.3 FY 2020/21 Overall Budget

The approved budget for the FY 2020/21 was Kshs.3.29 trillion, comprising Kshs.2.28 trillion for recurrent expenditure, Kshs.633.31 billion for development expenditure, and Kshs.369.87 billion towards financing county governments. This figure was revised to Kshs.3.42 trillion in the Supplementary Budget I comprising Kshs.2.35 trillion for recurrent expenditure, Kshs.696.57 billion for development and Kshs.369.87 billion to the county governments. In Supplementary Budget II, it was revised further to Kshs.3.42 trillion, comprising of Kshs.2.33 trillion for recurrent expenditure, Kshs.705.93 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.382.60 towards county governments.

3.3.4 Overdraft Facility
The overdraft (OD) facility is a temporary source of funds to cater for short-term needs, mainly to fund deficit in payments of domestic debt instruments such as the matured Treasury Bills .

The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) overdraft is restricted to a maximum of five per cent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year. Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act, 2012 specifies that;

'For the purposes of subsection (2)(c), short term borrowing shall be restricted to management of cash flows, and in case of a bank overdraft facility it shall not exceed five per cent of the most recent audited national government revenue'

In the FY 2020/21, the statement of audited revenues used to set the limit for the OD facility was that of the FY 2018/19 period as there was no substantive Auditor General in place to sign off the audited accounts for FY 2019/20. The limit set was Kshs 65 billion up to the third quarter of FY 2020/21 but was revised to Kshs 75 billion after the new Auditor General signed the audited accounts of FY 2019/20.

In the FY 2020/21, the total charges on the overdraft facility were Kshs.2.21 billion, charged at 7 per cent per annum on the amounts outstanding at the end of every month. Table 3.4 shows a breakdown of the costs incurred during the year in the utilization of the OD facility.

blocks.text: 4.3 Education Sector

The Education sector is mandated to provide quality education, training, science, technology, research and skills development. The sector's overall goal is to increase access to education and training, improve the quality and relevance of education, reduce inequality, and leverage knowledge and skills in science, technology, and innovation for global competitiveness. It also envisions contributing to the achievement of the 'Big Four Agenda' by providing the requisite skilled human resources and promoting research and development.

The State Department for Post Training and Skills Development had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.126.07 million (less than 1 per cent of the sector's budget). This is attributed to its mandate to provide an institutional framework to devise and implement national, sectoral, and workplace strategies to develop and improve the skills of the Kenyan workforce and management of talents and post-training policy. heading_path: 4.5 Environmental Protection, Water and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: 6.1 Introduction

This chapter highlights the critical issues identified as having affected budget implementation in the FY 2020/21. Further, it provides recommendations aimed at improving budget implementation in the future.
6.2 Key Issues and Recommendations

In overseeing budget implementation in the FY 2020/21, the OCoB identified the following issues that hampered budget implementation, namely high levels of public debt, pending bills, non-adherence to end of year cut-off timelines, late supplementary budgets, and delays in submission of reports to the OCoB. The issues are detailed hereunder.
6.2.1  High Levels of Public Debt

Article 201(c) of the Constitution of Kenya stipulates that the burdens and benefits of using resources and public borrowing shall be shared equitably between present and future generations. In addition, Section 50 (1) of the PFM Act, 2012 states; 'In guaranteeing and borrowing money, the national government shall ensure that its financing needs and payment obligations are at the lowest possible cost in the market, which is consistent with a prudent degree of risk while ensuring that the overall level of public debt is sustainable'.

OCOB has noted that public debt stock has recorded significant growth over recent years, attributed to a persistent shortfall in expected ordinary revenue and rising expenditures, therefore, occasioning the need for deficit financing. As of 30th June 2021, total public debt stock stood at Kshs.7.71 trillion. The total debt was comprised of 52.1 per cent external and 47.9 per cent domestic debt, representing a 15.2 per cent growth from Kshs.6.69 trillion as of 30th June 2020.

The total expenditure on public debt during FY 2020/21 was Kshs.765.91 billion, representing 80.2 per cent of the revised annual estimates, recording a growth from Kshs.717.65 billion recorded in FY 2019/20. This outturn is due to an increase in the principal repayments of both domestic and external debt and growth in interest payments on domestic debt.

To ensure compliance with the principles of public finance on sustainable financing, the government should devise and implement strategies to enhance ordinary revenue generation while reducing expenditures. Further, the government's borrowings should be used only for financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure and at the minimum cost to reduce the high cost associated with debt repayment.
6.2.2 Pending Bills

As of 30th June 2021, the MDAs pending bills stood at Kshs.36.35 billion, accounting for 5.1 per cent of the development budget for the year. Accumulation of pending bills by the affects the overall liquidity in the economy, especially that of the private sector, hence negatively impacting the overall economic growth.

The public finance management framework requires that pending bills are settled timeously as specified in contract agreements to avoid the accumulation of arrears. Accordingly, all pending bills should be budgeted as a first charge and paid without delay as provided for under Regulation 42(1a) of Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations, 2015. The Regulation states that 'debt service payments shall be a first charge on the Consolidated Fund and the Accounting Officer shall ensure this is done to the extent possible, so that the government does not default on debt obligations'.

Based on the foregoing, the Controller of Budget recommends that all MDAs ensure payment of pending bills is prioritised as a first charge in the FY 2021/22 in compliance with the law to avoid further accumulation of pending bills and enhance liquidity and growth of the economy.
6.2.3 Non-Adherence to end of financial year timelines
heading_path: 6.2.3 Non-Adherence to end of financial year timelines

blocks.text: The OCoB noted that some Exchequer issues relating to the FY 2020/21 and financial transactions continued to be made through the first half of July 2021, which falls in the FY 2021/22 period. The last Exchequer requisition for FY 2020/21 was made by the National Treasury on 9th July, 2021 Considering the related expenditure was captured in the FY 2020/21 period, it implies that the IFMIS system remained open to capture FY 2020/21 expenditure well into the first half of July 2021.
heading_path: 6.2.3 Non-Adherence to end of financial year timelines

blocks.text: Failure to observe the financial year closing timelines of 30th June poses a challenge since the Supplementary Appropriation Act, 2021 had lapsed on 30th June 2021. Section 45(1) of the Public Finance Management (PFM) Act, 2012 states that 'An appropriation that has not been spent at the end of the financial year for which it was appropriated shall lapse immediately at the end of that financial year'.
heading_path: 6.2.3 Non-Adherence to end of financial year timelines

blocks.text: Accordingly, the National Treasury should establish and adhere to end-of-year cut-off procedures and ensure that the release and utilisation of funds are based on an existing Appropriation Act.
heading_path: 6.2.3 Non-Adherence to end of financial year timelines

blocks.text: 6.2.4  Late Supplementary Budget

In the FY 2020/21, the National Treasury presented two Supplementary Budgets for approval by the National Assembly. The supplementary budgets were intended to realign budget allocations from non-core activities to core activities to promote the economy's recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic.

However, the second Supplementary Budget was assented to on 29th June 2021, which was too close to the end of the financial year and did not allow adequate time to implement the revisions. Further, analysis of reports from MDAs showed that some reported absorption rates above 100 per cent, attributed to budget cuts above the expenditure already incurred. While budget cuts may be necessary, the National Treasury should consider actual expenditure and commitments at the time of any revision to avoid reducing budgetary allocations below the cumulative expenditure and commitments. In addition, Supplementary Budgets should not be approved too close to year-end. MDAs may not have adequate time to implement planned activities when budget revisions are approved too close to year-end.

The COB recommends that the National Treasury should liaise with MDAs before effecting budget revisions and appropriately align budget allocations to ensure that they do not exceed the incurred expenditure, interfering with critical programmes in the MDAs. The National Treasury should prepare Supplementary Budgets in good time while Parliament should consider and approve budget revisions early enough to implement planned activities.
6.2.5  Delay in the submission of Financial Reports to OCoB
heading_path: 6.2.5  Delay in the submission of Financial Reports to OCoB

blocks.text: Article 228 (6) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016 requires the Controller of Budget to submit a report to each House of Parliament on the implementation of budgets of the national and county governments every four months. The Controller of Budget report is based on reports on financial and non-financial performance submitted by MDAs in line with Section 83 of the PFM Act, 2012.
heading_path: 6.2.5  Delay in the submission of Financial Reports to OCoB

blocks.text: The OCoB noted delays in submitting the annual reports on financial and non-financial performance by some MDAs. The reports were due by 15th July 2021, in line with Section 83 of the PFM Act, 2012. Failure to submit reports on time affected timely reporting and the oversight of budget implementation by various stakeholders.
heading_path: 6.2.5  Delay in the submission of Financial Reports to OCoB

blocks.text: Accounting Officers should submit financial and non-financial performance reports to the OCoB within fifteen days following the end of each quarter to facilitate timely preparation and publication of budget implementation reports.
heading_path: 6.2.5  Delay in the submission of Financial Reports to OCoB

blocks.text: 6.2.6  Over-absorption of Budget by MDAs

Analysis of reports submitted to the OCoB by MDAs, we noted expenditure for some budget lines exceeded the budget amount while others within the same vote recorded low absorption. This over absorption of funds is attributed to budget cuts during the Supplementary Budgets which are effected when expenditure on the budget item has been incurred. This should be regularised in the subsequent Supplementary Budget.

The COB recommends Accounting Officers of the affected MDAs to liaise with National Treasury to ensure that, the under-utilised budget lines are reallocated to other budget items and overdrawn budget lines are corrected before the end of the financial year.
7  EMERGING ISSUES

This budget implementation review report aims at presenting the budget performance by the national government in the FY 2020/21. To inform and improve future efforts in budget implementation, it is necessary to highlight the emerging issues that have been identified to either affect the credibility of the budget or pose various risks in implementation of the budgets.
7.1 Introduction

Successful budget implementation is a critical determinant for successful delivery of the government agenda. For effective implementation of the government policies and programmes, the approved budgets should be both credible and reliable. The credibility of budgets is essential during both the formulation and implementation of the approved budgets. For any budget to be deemed credible, it must be characterised by minimum revisions and reallocation of funds to or from the approved programmes during the implementation process.

Budget implementation during the reporting period was characterised by supplementary funding requests and reallocations of the approved budgets arising from the MDAs' requests. The frequent requests for supplementary funding can potentially undermine the approved budgets' credibility and reliability.

Article 223 of the Constitution sets out conditions when requests for additional funding may be permitted which include unforeseen emergencies occurring during budget implementation, lack of funding for projects in the approved budgets, amongst other factors. It has, however, been observed that several MDAs have relied on Article 223 to make requests for funds for activities that are not of an emergency nature. Therefore, this section provides an analysis of the total requests for supplementary funding, including the actual additional funds received during the period. It also highlights other issues identified during the period that can negatively impact the budget implementation process.

blocks.text: 7.3 Effects of Continued Reliance on External Borrowing on Budget Implemen -tation
heading_path: 7.3 Effects of Continued Reliance on External Borrowing on Budget Implemen -tation

blocks.text: The stock of public and publicly guaranteed debt stock increased from Kshs 6.20 trillion (65.6 percent of Gross Domestic Product) in June 2020 to Kshs 7.71 trillion (65.8 percent of Gross Domestic Product) in June 2021, representing an increase of Kshs1.51 trillion. To deal with the high debt repayment levels, the government requested and received debt relief on Kshs.77.8 billion to address the COVID-19 pandemic. The continued reliance on external borrowing has negatively impacted the government's commitment to reduce expenditures and maintain the overall borrowing within sustainable levels in line with Article 201 of the Constitution. Further, external borrowing depletes the country's foreign exchange reserves, at a time when the Kenya shilling has been unfavourably impacted.
heading_path: 7.3 Effects of Continued Reliance on External Borrowing on Budget Implemen -tation

blocks.text: To manage the rising public debt, the Controller of Budget recommends that the government continue rationalising expenditures on recurrent activities, especially foreign travel, and re-evaluate spending on less critical development activities. In addition, the government should explore other revenue-raising measures to enhance local revenue mobilization.
heading_path: 7.3 Effects of Continued Reliance on External Borrowing on Budget Implemen -tation

blocks.text: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: There were instances where revenue from Loans & Grants meant to fund development activities was applied to the recurrent budget and to disbursements to Counties. The following are instances where the government applied borrowed funds towards recurrent and development budgets in the FY 2020/21.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: (i) On 22nd June 2021, the National Treasury received Kshs.80.78 billion from the International Monetary Fund as a semi-concessional loan for budget support. However, the analysis of available data shows that Kshs.105.05 million from the total funds received was used to fund recurrent activities in the approved national government budget. (ii) On 30th June 2021, the government received a total of Kshs.70.17 billion from Sovereign Bond Proceeds (external borrowing) relating to the State Department for Infrastructure, the State Department for Water, Sanitation and Irrigation, the State Department for Housing, Urban Development, and the State Department for ICT & Innovation. The available data shows that the National Treasury used Kshs.18.16 billion out of the borrowed funds to support recurrent activities in the approved national government budget.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: The two examples provide instances where the government contravened Article 201(c) of the Constitution and Section 15(2) (c) of the PFM Act, 2012, which states that 'over the medium term, the national government's borrowings shall be used only for the purpose of financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure'.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: To ensure adherence to the approved budgets and promote prudence in the use of public funds, the Controller of Budget recommends that the National Treasury should ensure public funds are spent in line with Article 201(c) of the Constitution and Section 15(2) (c) of the PFM Act, 2012.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: This report sought to provide budget performance for the National Government in the FY 2020/21 covering the period July 2020 to June 2021, pursuant to Article 228 of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act. The report provided progress on budget implementation by the National Government in terms of funding, implementation of planned programmes and issues affecting budget execution.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: Budget implementation in the FY 2020/21 showed resilience in the Kenyan economy in spite of the uncertain global effects of the social and economic environment caused by the spread of COVID-19 pandemic. Revenues into the Consolidated Fund Services recorded a growth of 9.3 per cent over those of FY 2019/20. The growth is attributed to sustained compliance efforts, revenue enhancement initiatives and improved voluntary compliance by taxpayers, among other initiatives by KRA. However, there is a need to widen the tax base in order to add the number of tax paying citizens especially in the informal sector.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: Total exchequer issues to MDAs amounted to Kshs.2.42 trillion representing 94.82 per cent of the revised net estimates against a target 100 per cent, a growth compared to 92.8 per cent recorded in FY 2019/20. Notably, the report noted growth in exchequer issues over the FY 2019/20 except on the Consolidated Fund Services which recorded a marginal decline.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: Total expenditure for the national government was Kshs.2.52 trillion representing an absorption rate of 85.4 per cent, a decline compared to 88.9 per cent recorded in the FY 2019/20. The Development budget recorded the lowest absorption at 79.5 per cent a decline from 86.2 per cent while the recurrent budget recorded an absorption rate of 87.2 per cent, a decline compared to 89.8 per cent recorded in the FY 2019/20 respectively. Decline on absorption of funds is attributed to late approval of the Supplementary Budget II towards the end of the financial year and MDAs were therefore not able to implement some of the planned activities towards the end of the year. Secondly, due to resurgence of the COVID-19, MDAs planned activities were affected by mitigation measures introduced by the government to curb its spread. Activities affected included, among others travel, trainings and hospitality which form the highest percentage of operations and maintenance expenses.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: In overseeing the budget, the Controller of Budget identified key challenges and made recommendations aimed at addressing them. Although borrowing is allowed in the Constitution, the government should ensure that borrowing is used only for financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure and at the minimum cost to reduce the high cost associated with debt repayment. On outstanding pending bills, all MDAs should ensure payment of pending bills is prioritised as the first charge in the FY 2021/22 in compliance with the law to avoid further accumulation of pending bills and enhance liquidity and growth of the private sector.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: The Controller of Budget noted delays in submitting the quarterly reports on financial and non-financial performance by some MDAs. Failure to submit reports on time affected timely reporting and the oversight of budget implementation by various stakeholders. Accounting Officers should submit financial and nonfinancial performance reports to the OCOB within fifteen days following the end of each quarter to facilitate timely preparation and publication of budget implementation reports.
heading_path: 7.4 Funding of Recurrent Budget from Loans & Grants

blocks.text: The Controller of Budget encourages all the relevant oversight institutions and officers in government to ensure the implementation of the recommendations herein for effective budget implementation. Eventually, collaborative effort will lead to attainment of the national development objectives and goals as envisioned in the development blue-print, Vision 2030 and the Medium -Term Plan of the 'Big Four Agenda'.
